newsitem.title: USA: Frequent flyer miles are currency for fantasy awards.
newsitem.headline: Frequent flyer miles are currency for fantasy awards.

text.p: Frequent flyer miles, created to keep you hooked on an airline, seem worthless unless you accumulate enough to get a free air ticket.
But for jet-setting business travelers, yet another trip on a packed airplane is hardly a bonus after months of wearying travel.
Airlines' answer -- free miles for such unlikely deals as your mortgage payment, home purchases and cash advances on your credit card. And rewards that money cannot buy.

Like a chance to be Circus Ringmaster of The Greatest Show on Earth in the city of your choice. Or Honorary Coach of the Harlem Globetrotters. How about a private skating lesson by Nancy Kerrigan? Or hammering nails with former President Jimmy Carter to build a home for a needy family?

All these awards are yours for an estimated 100,000 to 300,000 Northwest Airlines miles at the carrier's DreamPerks Auction at Sotheby's on Friday. If you lack the miles to bid, you can buy them for 5 cents a mile, making the 35 fantasy awards worth $5,000 to $15,000 each. Most of the packages include first class flights and luxury lodgings for two.
Northwest, which has 15 million mileage holders, will donate proceeds mainly to Habitat for Humanity International to build homes for the needy worldwide.

"Frequent flyer miles have become a kind of de facto currency," said David Redden, senior vice president and director of Sotheby's New York. "You need creativity to spend the miles. This is a mechanism for dealing with that dilemma."
Airlines are wracking their brains to reward you for flying with them because, despite the cost, it's better than losing a customer to a competitor.

American Airlines now allows members to earn one mile for every dollar of interest paid on a new mortgage with one of five lenders. Consumers can also earn 15,000 miles for every $100,000 of the purchase or sale price of a home when using a participating real estate broker.
For example, the sale of a $150,000 home would earn 22,500 miles -- more than enough for a coach flight within the continental United States (20,000 miles).
Even payments for such mundane services as lawn mowing, carpet cleaning or housekeeping will now earn miles, not to mention telephone and credit card bills.

Awards are now easier to earn because some require fewer than the 15,000 miles needed for free air tickets or upgrades. American Airline now offers one-night stays at major hotel chains for as few as 10,000 miles and a two-day weekday or three-day weekend car rental for 12,000 miles.

In other words, frequent flyer mile programmes are here to stay. And, in case you didn't know, miles on Continental, USAir and Delta Air Lines do not expire. So it pays to treat them as currency you can shop with, accumulate sweat-free and even use for retirement. And compare programmes.
"Consumers always screw up and assume all programmes are created equal," said Randy Peterson, editor and publisher ofo Inside Flyer magazine (800-209-2870) in Colorado Springs, Colo.
"Do you want a free ticket to Hawaii? If so, choose an airline that goes there. USAir does not."

If do not fly a lot, get on a programme with miles that don't expire, because it could take you four or five years to earn a free trip. Stick with an airline instead of scattering your miles among rivals.

This is especially important for frequent flyers because most airlines offer special perks like free upgrades, bonus miles and advance boarding to consumers who fly 25,000 miles or more a year on the carrier.

Accumulate miles faster on land by charging purchases on an affiliated credit, and using a long distance phone carrier that offers free miles. For example, American Express card holders earn miles that can be used on Delta, Continental, USAir, Aeromexico, Swissair, Sabena and Southwest Airlines.
MCI Communications Corp. lets you earn free travel on American, Continental, Northwest or Southwest Airlines.
"Get the most value from your miles instead of just using them" anyhow, said Peterson, who also publishes "The Official Frequent Flyer Guidebook" which compares programmes.

For example, don't waste 25,000 miles to redeem a roundtrip ticket from New York to Pittsburgh, worth about $150, when you could fly as far as the West Coast. For another 5,000 to 10,000 miles, you could go to Europe.

"Remember that programmes these days are complex, with wide variety of partners," said Peterson. "The fastest way to a free award is by understanding the partners. In most instances, you're not paying more. You just have to be a wise consumer like in any other investment."
